terms.comment: The modern word, a diminutive of sigārum, cigar. A packet of cigarettes is capsella sigarellōrum (Traupman 291).

terms.gloss: a cigarette (a little stick of tobacco)
terms.comment: A description on classical bacillum, a little stick; tobacco is tabācum (Morgan–Owens, after Linnaeus).

evidence: M-O s.v. smoke vb. (cigarettes, etc.): fūmum (alicujus reī) haurīre
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase; Morgan–Owens gives fūmum haurīre from eighteenth- and nineteenth-century writers, and Egger’s no-smoking sign, ubi fūmus haurīrī vetātur.

terms.gloss: a cigarette (as some modern Latinists use it)
terms.comment: Morgan–Owens warns that fistula, a tube, fits a pipe, not a cigarette, and was so used of pipes in earlier centuries.

sigarum.html: Morgan–Owens s.v. cigar writes sigârum. With the long vowel the Latin stress falls where Spanish cigarro, the source of the word, has it, as the house does for modern names with no Latin quantity (Lisbōna).

sources: Lewis & Short: bacillum · Lewis & Short: fistula · Lewis & Short: haurio
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 291, 381, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
